implementation_notes: The canonical realization is hand-written: a per-type class holding a member per constructor parameter, initialised to commonly used values in the declarations, chainable withEmail(...) methods that return *this, and a terminal build() that constructs the product through its real constructor (or its private constructor via friendship). Static factory functions (aUser(), anInvoice()) are the syntactic sugar that makes tests read like the domain, and a but() that copies the builder lets tests derive a similar object. Use this form when the product is not an aggregate, when construction carries invariants or multi-step setup, or when the team wants the builder explicit and discoverable.
pitfalls: Builder defaults duplicated from the product's constructor drift apart; derive them from one factory (aUser()) or from the product's own defaults instead of repeating literals.

withX() returning *this is safe only while build() is const and the builder owns its members: returning references into temporaries, or handing one builder to two tests, yields dangling or shared state.

variants.name: Aggregate with default member initializers (C++20 designated initializers)
variants.implementation_notes: Give every member a default member initializer and let the aggregate itself be the valid instance: a test then writes User{ .email = "bad@example.com" } and mentions nothing else, or copies a valid instance and assigns to one member. The builder class disappears, because C++20 designated initializers plus default member initializers provide both of the builder's steps directly in the language. Choose this variant while construction is a plain aggregate; switch to the fluent builder once construction must be conditional, validated or step-wise, since an aggregate may not have private members, user-declared constructors or invariants of its own.
pitfalls: Designated initializers must follow declaration order and reject narrowing, and any member left out silently keeps its default - which is the point, but a default the domain would reject is then just as invisible to tests as to production code.
Aggregates cannot enforce invariants (no private members, no user-declared constructors), so validation must move into a named constructor or checking function that tests also call.
